The False herring (Harengula clupeola) attains a maximum adult body size of 22.5 cm [Li = 22.5 cm] in total length, a value recorded from extensive field surveys throughout its western Atlantic range. This clupeid species typically reaches sexual maturation at a total length of 11 cm [Lp = 11 cm], marking the onset of gonad development and the transition to a reproductively viable adult. The initiation of spawning events in this population is tightly linked to warm seasonal temperatures; under the stable water temperature of 26.7 °C [T = 26.7 °C], laboratory studies have documented that newly hatched larvae emerge from the egg at approximately 12 days [ab = approximately 12 days] post-fertilization, an interval reflecting the rapid embryogenesis characteristic of tropical clupeids. This hatching duration, measured under controlled conditions, provides a baseline for understanding larval emergence in the wild, where thermal variability can alter developmental rates considerably.

The wet weight at birth for newly emerged yolk-sac larvae of Harengula clupeola is approximately 0.0024 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0024 grams], a minute mass that underscores the substantial investment in fecundity over individual offspring size typical of small pelagic spawners. Subsequent growth is rapid, with juveniles transitioning from a planktonic larval phase to a more robust juvenile morphology. Based on length-weight regressions derived from regional stock assessments, the ultimate wet weight of an adult False herring reaches 123.4 grams [Wwi = 123.4 grams], a value that represents the asymptotic mass for fully grown individuals. This substantial increase in biomass from the larval stage to adulthood is accompanied by a shift in habitat use, as post-metamorphic juveniles move from open pelagic waters into more structured coastal environments where food resources are abundant.

Reproductive output in False herring is considerable, with mature females producing a high number of eggs per spawning event. Observations of the congeneric species Harengula humeralis indicate that the maximum reproductive rate in this genus is achieved at a temperature of 26.7 °C [T = 26.7 °C], with each female shedding approximately 110 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 110 eggs per day] across the spawning season. This output reflects the group's strategy of high fecundity and broadcast spawning in coastal waters. Although the actual reproductive investment, when broken down as approximately 110 eggs per day, translates into a substantial seasonal reproductive output, the realized fecundity varies with food availability and population density.

The wet weight at puberty for female Harengula clupeola, estimated from the length-weight relationship of 0.00871 times length to the power of 3.07, is 13.7 grams [Wwp = 13.7 grams]. This mass marks the threshold at which individuals begin directing resources toward gamete production, and it typically coincides with the attainment of a total length of 11 cm [Lp = 11 cm], as noted earlier. The transition from juvenile to pubertal stage involves not only a change in body composition but also the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, which drives vitellogenesis and spermiation. In wild populations, individuals reaching this mass during the warm summer months are predicted to contribute to the first major spawning pulse of the year, synchronizing their reproductive efforts with peak zooplankton abundance.

Longevity data for False herring, derived from otolith-based age estimates, indicate that the maximum lifespan in the species is approximately 7 years [am = approximately 7 years] when maintained at a stable water temperature of 26.7 °C [T = 26.7 °C]. This relatively short lifespan, when compared to other clupeids of similar body size, is consistent with the fast life-history pace of small-bodied clupeids, which prioritize early maturation and high fecundity over extended somatic maintenance. Senescent declines in body condition and reproductive output become evident after the fifth year, and by that point, most individuals have succumbed to natural mortality, predation, or the energetic costs of repeated spawning events. The species thus exemplifies a classic r-selected strategy, balancing a brief adult phase against a high per-capita reproductive output across its available spawning seasons.
